meta.description: Inflection-point pool for the vr-immersion theme. Originally ported from VR_Speculation's pastcasting milestone data (17 points). Expanded with: a pre-1952 prehistory of immersive spectacle (panorama, diorama, stereoscope, early cinema, Hale's Tours, sound film, pre-Cinerama 3D and panoramic-projection experiments); a computer-graphics bridge thread that crosses between the Sutherland (engineering) and Heilig (cinematic/somatic) lineages (BEFLIX, Lucasfilm/Pixar, Videoplace, Osmose); and a 2013-2026 arc covering Oculus's absorption into Facebook/Meta, the metaverse rebrand and retreat, and the arrival of generative world models (Genie, World Labs).

milestones.label: Barker's Panorama
milestones.description: Robert Barker patents 'Apparatus for Exhibiting Pictures' and in 1788 exhibits the world's first full-circle panorama, a 360-degree view of Edinburgh from Calton Hill, in a purpose-built rotunda. Viewers stand on a raised central platform with sightlines controlled top and bottom so they cannot see where the painting ends. The first engineered apparatus built specifically to surround the visual field and blur where the image stops and reality begins — the starting point of a 190-year project of visual-immersion engineering that runs through Cinerama and into this pool's existing milestones.

branch_alternatives.description: Barker or an early follower mechanizes the panorama — a moving canvas, mechanical lighting or weather effects — decades before Daguerre's diorama introduces animation, collapsing the panorama/diorama distinction into a single continuous invention.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Engineering investment in moving-canvas or mechanical-effects infrastructure within Barker's own rotunda business
downstream_effects: The diorama's defining innovation (animated light and time-of-day effects) arrives decades earlier and is credited to Barker's tradition rather than treated as Daguerre's separate invention
The panorama-diorama lineage merges into one continuous project rather than splintering into two named media
Static panorama painting loses its status as the format's original, 'pure' form

milestones.label: Daguerre's Diorama
milestones.description: Louis Daguerre, working in the panorama tradition, opens the Diorama in Paris: large-scale paintings animated from behind the screen with shifting light to simulate the passage of time — dawn breaking, weather changing. Still purely visual and purely passive, but a genuine ancestor of both cinema and theatrical special effects, and the first entry in this pool to add temporal change to an otherwise static immersive image.

milestones.label: Wheatstone's Reflecting Stereoscope
milestones.description: Charles Wheatstone demonstrates that presenting each eye with a slightly different 2D image produces a compelling illusion of 3D depth. Establishes stereopsis as the primary technology for visual immersion. Begins a 190-year project of visual-depth enhancement.

milestones.label: Holmes's Handheld Stereoscope
milestones.description: Oliver Wendell Holmes designs a cheap, simplified handheld stereoscope and deliberately leaves it unpatented to maximize adoption. Within a decade, stereoview cards of travel destinations, historical events, and staged domestic scenes are a fixture of middle-class parlors. The first mass-market immersive-visual object in this pool, and a deliberate act of openness rather than enclosure.

branch_alternatives.description: Holmes patents his simplified stereoscope design and licenses it for a fee rather than deliberately leaving it open, prioritizing personal profit over popular-science advocacy.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Holmes or his business partner Joseph Bates deciding the design's commercial value outweighs the goal of mass diffusion
downstream_effects: Mass stereo-photography culture develops more slowly and at higher cost through the 1860s-1900s
A licensing-fee model becomes an early, influential precedent for later visual-media patents in this pool, including the 1891 anaglyph patent
Stereoscopic viewing stays a more exclusive, upper-middle-class practice for longer, delaying its role as shared visual common ground

milestones.label: Edison's Kinetoscope
milestones.description: William K. L. Dickson, working for Edison, completes the Kinetoscope: a peephole viewing cabinet that lets one person at a time watch a short looping film by cranking and peering in. First commercial exhibition April 1894, New York. Solitary, private, coin-operated. No projection, no shared audience, no screen.

milestones.label: Ducos du Hauron's Anaglyph Patent
milestones.description: French scientist Louis Ducos du Hauron patents the anaglyph: separating an image into two color channels, viewed through correspondingly colored glasses, to reproduce stereo depth in a single printed or projected image. The technical basis for every red-green 3D film this pool's later 1922-1955 entries depend on.

milestones.label: Lumière Cinématographe
milestones.description: Auguste and Louis Lumière's lightweight Cinématographe both films and projects. In December 1895, Paris, they present the first projected moving pictures to a paying, shared audience — fairgrounds, music halls, darkened rooms, with live music and audience participation. The decisive fork against Edison's solitary peephole model: cinema becomes, from this point, a collective and theatrical medium rather than a private one.

branch_alternatives.description: Edison successfully patents and defends projection technology, or the Lumières fail to secure exhibition venues in Paris, and the solitary peephole-viewing model remains commercially dominant instead of shared theatrical projection.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Stronger Edison patent enforcement in Europe, or a failure of the Lumières' 1895 Paris exhibition to draw paying crowds
downstream_effects: Cinema develops as a private, individual-viewing medium rather than a collective theatrical one, closer in social shape to the later Walkman, arcade cabinet, or VR headset
The entire twentieth-century model of cinema-as-shared-public-event does not take hold in this form; something closer to arcade-parlor culture becomes the default
When collective, theatrical viewing does eventually emerge, if it does, it arrives through a different technological lineage than projection

milestones.label: Hale's Tours of the World
milestones.description: Movie houses built as full-scale replica train carriages, seating up to 72 passengers, with front-of-train footage projected at one end, steam-whistle and wheel sound effects, fans blowing bursts of wind from the rear, and painted scenery rolling past the side windows. First exhibited Kansas City, May 1905; 500 US locations at its 1907 peak. A full multisensory, kinesthetic cinema experience fifty years before Sensorama, and structurally its closest ancestor in this pool.

branch_alternatives.description: Rather than a five-year novelty fading by 1910, Hale's Tours' multisensory, kinesthetic exhibition format becomes the default template for movie-house construction, and fixed-seat flat-screen theaters develop as the minority format instead.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Continued investor confidence and content variety (not just train footage) sustaining audience interest past its historical novelty period
downstream_effects: The Heilig lineage's founding claim — that cinema must address the whole body, not just the eyes — has thirty years of commercial proof-of-concept before Heilig even publishes 'El Cine del Futuro' in 1955
Sensorama (1962) and the Experience Theater proposal (1964) read as continuations of an established commercial tradition rather than isolated inventions rejected by institutions
Cinema architecture and exhibitor economics through the mid-twentieth century are built around motion, wind, and sound infrastructure rather than optics and screen size alone

milestones.label: The Power of Love
milestones.description: The first 3D feature film, exhibited in anaglyph red/green at the Ambassador Hotel Theater in Los Angeles. Commercially unsuccessful — color balance is difficult to maintain and audiences find the glasses uncomfortable — and 3D filmmaking remains largely experimental for the next three decades rather than becoming a normalized part of Hollywood production.

branch_alternatives.description: The Power of Love's anaglyph presentation solves its color-balance and eyestrain problems well enough to become a commercial hit, and 3D filmmaking becomes a normalized part of 1920s Hollywood rather than a curiosity abandoned until the 1950s.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Better dye and filter stability for the red/green glasses, or immediate studio reinvestment following a strong opening
downstream_effects: This pool's existing '3D Film Golden Era' (1952-1955) happens thirty years early, and by the time it would historically have occurred it reads as a nostalgic revival rather than a first wave
Polarized 3D research (this pool's 1936-1939 entries) gets funded a decade earlier since anaglyph's commercial viability is already proven
Sound-film conversion (1926-1927) competes directly with an already-established 3D-film industry for capital and screen time, changing which innovation Hollywood prioritizes first

milestones.label: Vitaphone / Don Juan
milestones.description: Warner Bros. and Western Electric's Vitaphone sound-on-disc system debuts with Don Juan: no spoken dialogue, but nine synchronized discs of orchestral score and sound effects, recorded live and precisely matched to the reels. The first entry in this pool's cinema thread to add a genuinely new sensory channel — hearing — to what had been a purely visual medium.

milestones.label: The Jazz Singer
milestones.description: The first feature with synchronized spoken dialogue — only about a quarter of the film, but enough to end the silent era. Al Jolson's 'You ain't heard nothin' yet!' becomes the birth-cry of the talkies. Built on Vitaphone's fragile sound-on-disc system, which will lose the format war to sound-on-film (Movietone) within two years because discs kept drifting out of sync.

branch_alternatives.description: Fox's Movietone sound-on-film process reaches commercial maturity and wide rollout before Warner Bros' Vitaphone captures the 'first talkie' narrative with The Jazz Singer, so the industry standardizes on sound-on-film from the outset.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Movietone's studio and distribution rollout outpacing Vitaphone's marketing and exhibition push in 1926-1927
downstream_effects: Theaters avoid several years of costly, unreliable disc-projector synchronization infrastructure entirely
The transition to sound is faster and cheaper industry-wide, since prints rather than fragile discs carry the audio track
Warner Bros. loses its historical claim to having 'invented' the talkies, changing which studio dominates the sound-conversion decade that follows

milestones.label: Polarized 3D Features
milestones.description: Beggars' Wedding (Italy, 1936) is the first sound stereoscopic feature and the first to use polarized filters rather than anaglyph color separation, solving the color-fringing and eyestrain problems that sank The Power of Love. In Tune With Tomorrow (1939) brings polarized 3D to American screens. Technically solves what anaglyph could not, but the Depression and the onset of WWII restrict industry investment, and 3D remains a marginal format until the pool's 1952 'Golden Era.'

branch_alternatives.description: A major US studio invests in polarized-projection infrastructure immediately following In Tune With Tomorrow, rather than the format being sidelined by the Depression and the coming war.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Studio capital available for exhibition-hardware investment in the late 1930s despite the economic and political climate
downstream_effects: This pool's '3D Film Golden Era' (1952-1955) happens roughly fifteen years earlier and outside the postwar competition-with-television context that historically drove it
3D cinema's later reputation as 'a gimmick to compete with TV' never forms, since 3D predates mass television entirely in this branch
Heilig's 1955 manifesto, written as a critique of the historical 3D boom's collapse, either doesn't exist in this form or targets a completely different, earlier cultural moment

milestones.label: Fred Waller's Vitarama
milestones.description: Fred Waller's multi-projector panoramic system, shown at the 1939 World's Fair, uses several synchronized projectors and a curved screen to fill a wide field of view — the direct technical ancestor of this pool's 1952 Cinerama entry, and part of a flurry of realism-enhancing cinema experiments running from the 1920s through the early 1940s.

milestones.label: This is Cinerama
milestones.description: Widescreen Cinerama (three projectors, curved screen, 146-degree field of view, stereo surround sound) opens in New York to enormous success. Presence through visual scale and peripheral immersion rather than stereoscopic depth. A collective, theatrical, overwhelming spectacle.

branch_alternatives.description: Cinerama adds wind, vibration, and scent to its theatrical installations, building on the surround-sound precedent to address more sensory channels.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Entertainment industry interest in differentiating cinema from television through multisensory experience
downstream_effects: Multisensory cinema becomes a commercial standard before VR research begins
Heilig's Sensorama (1962) emerges into a market that already understands multisensory presence
Cinema engineering develops haptic infrastructure decades earlier

milestones.label: 3D Film Golden Era
milestones.description: Hollywood's first 3D boom: Bwana Devil (1952), House of Wax (1953), Creature from the Black Lagoon (1954), Dial M for Murder (1954). Over 50 3D features produced. The precise cultural context in which Heilig writes 'El Cine del Futuro' — he is critiquing cinema at its most immersively ambitious, arguing stereopsis alone is not enough.

branch_alternatives.description: The 3D golden era does not collapse in 1955 — improved polaroid systems solve sync and eyestrain problems, and 3D becomes the permanent default of Hollywood cinema.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Technical solutions to eyestrain and projector sync; continued studio investment
downstream_effects: Visual-only stereoscopic presence becomes the established cinema grammar
Heilig's somatic alternative has even less traction
The VR paradigm that eventually develops is even more visually centered

milestones.label: El Cine del Futuro (Heilig's Manifesto)
milestones.description: Morton Heilig publishes 'El Cine del Futuro' in a Mexican film journal. Argues that cinema must address all five senses to produce genuine presence. Written as the 3D boom collapses — Heilig diagnoses why: visual-only immersion is insufficient. Predates Sutherland's 'Ultimate Display' by a decade.

milestones.label: Heilig Telesphere Mask Patent
milestones.description: Heilig patents the Telesphere Mask — a head-mounted display for stereoscopic TV and film with stereo sound. Predates Sutherland's HMD by eight years. Unlike Sutherland's later HMD, it is designed for cinematic content rather than computer graphics, and is non-interactive.

branch_alternatives.description: A television network licenses the Telesphere Mask for home stereo TV broadcasts, making Heilig the pioneer of consumer HMDs rather than Sutherland.
branch_alternatives.requirement: TV industry interest in premium immersive content; manufacturing at scale
downstream_effects: HMD as consumer entertainment device enters homes in the 1960s
Development pressure on lightweight, comfortable HMD design begins two decades earlier
The HMD paradigm develops from cinematic content tradition, not CGI

milestones.label: Sensorama
milestones.description: Heilig builds the Sensorama — a coin-operated multisensory film booth with stereoscopic film, stereo sound, a vibrating seat, wind fans, and a scent dispenser. Five short films made. Uses 3D cinema as its visual substrate and augments it with the missing sensory channels. Cinematic, passive, somatic. No computer involvement.

branch_alternatives.description: An entertainment investor funds a chain of Sensorama arcade installations, building commercial infrastructure for multisensory cinema before VR research begins.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Entertainment investor interested in differentiating from TV
downstream_effects: Multisensory delivery infrastructure gets commercial engineering investment
Somatic presence becomes a commercial baseline, not an experimental curiosity

branch_alternatives.description: DARPA funds Heilig's multisensory work for human-factors and sensory environment research.
branch_alternatives.requirement: DARPA interest in full-sensorium simulation for training and research, parallel to their actual funding of Sutherland
downstream_effects: Somatic VR enters the military-industrial research pipeline
Develops toward training simulations rather than entertainment

milestones.label: Spacewar!
milestones.description: Martin Graetz, Wayne Witanen, and Steve Russell create Spacewar! at MIT — the first widely influential interactive computer game. Visual, two-player, competitive. Runs on a PDP-1 at MIT, the same institution and year as Sensorama, but in a completely different paradigm: interactive, computational, visual.

milestones.label: BEFLIX (Bell Labs Computer Animation)
milestones.description: Ken Knowlton, an engineer at Bell Labs, builds BEFLIX ('Bell Flicks') on an IBM 7090 mainframe with a Stromberg-Carlson SC4020 microfilm recorder — a FORTRAN/assembly system of graphic primitives (draw line, copy region, fill area, zoom) for producing raster computer animation. Engineers building batch-processed, algorithmic imagery, but naming and organizing it entirely around cinematic vocabulary: frames, scenes, cuts. Knowlton later collaborates with artist Stan VanDerBeek on the Poemfields films (1966-1969), pulling the work toward the art world even as Sutherland's Sketchpad (also 1963) and subsequent HMD research proceed on a nominally separate, MIT/Harvard-based engineering track in the same small, cross-aware community of early computer-graphics researchers.

branch_alternatives.description: Sutherland, aware of Bell Labs' work, directly incorporates BEFLIX's frame/scene/cut vocabulary and graphic-primitive approach into his own graphics research, rather than the two tracks staying institutionally separate.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Institutional cross-pollination between Bell Labs and MIT/Harvard's graphics programs — a shared conference, joint proposal, or personnel exchange
downstream_effects: The Sutherland lineage of computer graphics explicitly inherits cinematic editing vocabulary rather than developing a separate engineering vocabulary of primitives and transforms
Real-time interactive graphics and algorithmic/generative animation develop as a single hybrid discipline rather than splitting into separate fields for decades
The convergence of cinema and games/VR, which historically takes until machinima and virtual production in the 1990s-2000s, happens as early as the 1960s

branch_alternatives.description: Rather than remaining mostly an internal Bell Labs research and art tool, BEFLIX's graphic-primitive technique is published or licensed widely enough to become an early de facto standard for computer-generated visual effects in film and television.
branch_alternatives.requirement: AT&T (barred as a regulated monopoly from directly competing in consumer computing) choosing to publish the technique broadly, or an outside studio adopting it independently
downstream_effects: Computer-generated imagery enters commercial film and television production a decade or more before Tron (1982)
The 'graphic primitives' vocabulary, not the frame/scene/cut cinematic vocabulary, becomes the computer graphics industry's dominant technical language earlier
Bell Labs, rather than Lucasfilm/Pixar, becomes remembered as the seminal computer-animation studio

not_available: digital raster displays (output was microfilm/16mm film, not a screen)

milestones.label: Heilig Experience Theater Proposal
milestones.description: Heilig proposes a full-scale multisensory theater — a room-sized Sensorama for audiences. Rejected by investors and institutions. The failure was not technical but institutional: no capital, no research backing, no corporate champion. This is the moment the Heilig lineage effectively loses its chance at development.

branch_alternatives.description: The National Endowment for the Arts (or a foundation like Rockefeller) funds the Experience Theater as an experimental arts installation.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Arts funding bodies interested in expanded cinema and installation art (Happenings, Fluxus context)
downstream_effects: Somatic VR develops within the experimental arts world alongside Fluxus and expanded cinema
Its aesthetic vocabulary is avant-garde, not commercial

branch_alternatives.description: The Experience Theater is installed at a World's Fair (1964-65 New York World's Fair context) as a major attraction.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Corporate sponsor interested in immersive pavilion experience
downstream_effects: Somatic VR gets massive public exposure and corporate legitimacy
Public expectation for VR is set by the somatic paradigm rather than the CGI paradigm

milestones.label: The Ultimate Display (Sutherland)
milestones.description: Ivan Sutherland publishes 'The Ultimate Display' at IFIP. Imagines a computer display as a room in which the computer can control the existence of matter — presence through total visual illusion. The foundational imaginative blueprint for visual VR. Completely ignores smell, touch, taste.

milestones.label: Sword of Damocles (Sutherland HMD)
milestones.description: Sutherland builds the first computer-driven HMD at Harvard. Purely visual, wireframe-only graphics. So heavy it requires ceiling mounting — the 'Sword of Damocles.' Head-tracked. Sets the paradigm for visual-first, CGI-based VR for fifty years.

branch_alternatives.description: DARPA simultaneously funds a somatic/haptic track alongside Sutherland's visual work — treating them as two research streams in a single immersive environment program.
branch_alternatives.requirement: DARPA interest in full-sensorium simulation for pilot training
downstream_effects: Two paradigms develop with equivalent institutional resources through the 1970s
The 'VR headset' is not automatically the defining interface — haptic suits, scent chambers develop in parallel

milestones.label: Videoplace (Myron Krueger)
milestones.description: Myron Krueger builds Videoplace: video cameras capture participants' silhouettes and place them, in real time, into a shared computer-graphic space they can interact within — no goggles, no gloves, no wires. Krueger calls it 'artificial reality,' a term that predates 'virtual reality.' Public debut at the Milwaukee Art Museum, October 1975, funded by the National Endowment for the Arts and the Wisconsin Arts Board — the arts-institutional funding this pool's 1964 Heilig Experience Theater proposal imagined but never received, realized a decade later by a different inventor. Computational and real-time like Sutherland's track, full-body and unencumbered like Heilig's ambition: a genuine bridge between both lineages.

branch_alternatives.description: A toy or arcade-entertainment company licenses Krueger's camera-based full-body interaction system for commercial installations well before the Power Glove (1989) or Wii (2006), making markerless full-body computer vision a mainstream gaming interface fifteen to thirty years early.
branch_alternatives.requirement: A commercial investor recognizing arcade or entertainment potential in Krueger's NEA-funded research prototype, and camera/processing costs falling enough for commercial viability
downstream_effects: Full-body, wireless, camera-based interaction — the lineage that historically arrives commercially with Kinect in 2010 — becomes the dominant gaming interface paradigm from the late 1970s onward
The Power Glove (1989) and Wii (2006), both already in this pool, become minor footnotes rather than landmark firsts
Krueger, not Lanier or Sutherland, becomes the popularly remembered pioneer of interactive virtual environments

not_available: networked multi-site interaction beyond a lab-to-lab video link

milestones.label: Lucasfilm Computer Division Founded
milestones.description: George Lucas recruits Ed Catmull — a direct PhD student of Ivan Sutherland at the University of Utah's DARPA-funded computer graphics program, alongside fellow students Jim Clark and Alan Kay — to head a new Computer Division at Lucasfilm, tasked with bringing digital film editing, digital sound, and computer graphics into commercial filmmaking. The Sutherland engineering lineage, incubated inside defense-funded academic research, pivots explicitly toward Hollywood entertainment for the first time.

branch_alternatives.description: Catmull, instead of joining Lucasfilm, takes an academic or defense-contractor position continuing the DARPA-funded simulation/graphics work directly — flight simulation, NASA-adjacent work — rather than pivoting to commercial filmmaking.
branch_alternatives.requirement: No entertainment-industry recruiter makes an attractive offer, or Catmull's own interests stay closer to the simulation and training applications his Utah cohort was funded to pursue
downstream_effects: The Sutherland lineage's commercial expression in the 1980s stays defense/simulation-flavored rather than entertainment-flavored
Computer-generated imagery in commercial film is delayed by a decade or more, or is pioneered by a different, less Utah-DARPA-descended team
Steve Jobs never has a computer-graphics division to acquire in 1986; Pixar in its historical form does not exist

milestones.label: NASA VIEW Program
milestones.description: NASA Ames develops the Virtual Interface Environment Workstation (VIEW) — an HMD with DataGlove for telepresence and simulation. First major institutional application of visual VR after Sutherland. Establishes VR as a serious research and operational tool.

branch_alternatives.description: NASA VIEW program includes a parallel multisensory track — developing full-body haptic suits and olfactory interfaces alongside the visual HMD.
branch_alternatives.requirement: NASA interest in realistic simulation of planetary environments for astronaut training
downstream_effects: Full-body haptic suit gets NASA engineering resources in the 1980s
Military-grade somatic VR develops alongside visual VR

milestones.label: VPL Research / Jaron Lanier
milestones.description: Jaron Lanier founds VPL Research and coins 'virtual reality.' Produces the DataGlove (gesture interface) and EyePhone HMD. First commercial VR company. Primarily visual but the DataGlove introduces haptic gesture — a partial Heilig retrieval within the Sutherland paradigm. Expensive; professional/research market only.

branch_alternatives.description: VPL prioritizes the DataGlove somatic/haptic work over the EyePhone visual HMD — betting that gesture and touch interfaces are the key innovation.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Different investor priorities; medical/therapeutic market demand for haptic precision
downstream_effects: The defining VR technology of the late 1980s is the haptic glove, not the HMD
Consumer VR in the 1990s is haptic-first, not display-first

milestones.label: Nintendo Power Glove
milestones.description: Nintendo and Mattel release the Power Glove — a consumer gesture/haptic controller for the NES. Fails commercially (poor tracking accuracy, few compatible games). Becomes culturally iconic as a failed future. The first mass-market attempt to make gesture/body interface the gaming paradigm.

branch_alternatives.description: The Power Glove achieves accurate gesture tracking and Nintendo builds a substantial game library around it — establishing body-gesture as the dominant gaming interface 17 years before the Wii.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Better accelerometer technology; Nintendo commitment to game development for the format
downstream_effects: Gesture/body interface becomes the gaming default in the early 1990s
The somatic paradigm in gaming has a 10-year head start

milestones.label: Osmose (Char Davies)
milestones.description: Painter-turned-Softimage-VP Char Davies debuts Osmose at the Musée d'art contemporain de Montréal: a stereoscopic HMD and biometric vest whose only interface is breath and balance — exhaling sinks the immersant through a layered virtual landscape, inhaling lifts them. Built on the same HMD hardware lineage as Sutherland and VPL's research systems, but explicitly conceived by Davies as a corrective to what she called VR's masculine, militarized, conquest-oriented design language — replacing joysticks and gloves with the most involuntary, unconquerable interface available.

branch_alternatives.description: Osmose's breath/balance interface research is licensed or adapted by a VR hardware company as an input method alongside or instead of handheld controllers, rather than remaining a singular fine-art installation.
branch_alternatives.requirement: A VR hardware company investing in biometric sensing for consumer hardware rather than treating it as a one-off art-world experiment
downstream_effects: Consumer VR from the late 1990s onward includes biometric, involuntary-bodily input as a standard alongside hand controllers, rather than these appearing decades later in wellness-oriented VR
VR's popular design language incorporates Davies's explicit critique of conquest/mastery interaction models earlier and more broadly
Later controller-and-gesture-based headsets in this pool exist in a market that already expects a biometric option, changing their design briefs

milestones.label: Toy Story / Pixar's Fully Computer-Animated Feature
milestones.description: Sixteen years after Lucasfilm's Computer Division was founded, and nine years after Steve Jobs spun it off as Pixar (1986), Pixar releases Toy Story — the first entirely computer-animated feature film, roughly 800,000 render-hours, no traditional cel animation at any stage. A direct institutional and personal descendant of Sutherland's Sketchpad and the Utah DARPA program reaches mass-market Hollywood entertainment. Like every milestone in this Sutherland-descended thread, it is purely audiovisual — no haptic, olfactory, or other sensory channel is addressed, however emotionally 'present' the animated characters are made to feel.

branch_alternatives.description: Full CG animation proves commercially unconvincing at feature length in 1995 — rendering costs, character believability — and the industry instead settles for another decade on a hybrid model, CG effects and sequences embedded within traditionally animated or live-action films, rather than an all-CG feature.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Toy Story's character animation or box-office reception falling short of what made it convincing historically, or Disney hedging with a hybrid release strategy
downstream_effects: Fully computer-animated features arrive in the 2000s rather than 1995, delaying the reallocation of Hollywood animation labor and capital toward CG studios by a decade
Pixar itself, without Toy Story's proof-of-concept success, is acquired, absorbed, or wound down rather than becoming an independent powerhouse
Traditional 2D animation studios retain market and cultural dominance for longer, changing the competitive landscape Disney's own animation division operates in through the 1990s-2000s

milestones.label: Nintendo Wii
milestones.description: Nintendo releases the Wii with motion-controller interface. 100 million units sold. The most commercially successful example of somatic/body interface gaming. A partial Heilig retrieval: somatic presence without multisensory richness, but at mass-market scale.

branch_alternatives.description: Nintendo follows the Wii's somatic success by partnering with a VR researcher to produce a Wii VR headset that prioritizes body-motion interface over visual fidelity.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Nintendo strategic decision to leverage somatic success into immersive hardware before Oculus gets there
downstream_effects: Consumer VR in 2008-2010 is defined by motion-somatic interface rather than high-fidelity visual display
The Oculus Rift (2012) enters a market already shaped by somatic VR expectations

branch_alternatives.description: The Wii's success at somatic gaming triggers a wave of VR research funding aimed at multisensory somatic presence.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Research community recognizes the Wii as evidence for the Heilig paradigm; funding follows
downstream_effects: Somatic VR research gets a 6-year head start on visual VR research before Oculus appears
The haptic suit, not the headset, becomes the primary VR research challenge

milestones.label: Oculus Rift Kickstarter
milestones.description: Palmer Luckey launches the Oculus Rift on Kickstarter — using cheap smartphone OLED panels and IMU sensors to revive consumer VR. Pure visual paradigm. Acquired by Facebook for $2B in 2014. Arrives precisely as somatic gaming (Wii, Kinect) is retreating.

branch_alternatives.description: A parallel Kickstarter for a consumer haptic suit succeeds simultaneously with Oculus — establishing somatic and visual VR as co-equal consumer products from 2012 onward.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Kickstarter crowdfunding ecosystem for hardware; consumer appetite for somatic gaming after Wii
downstream_effects: Consumer VR from 2012 onward includes both visual and somatic paradigms as options
Facebook/Oculus acquisition does not automatically mean visual VR wins

milestones.label: John Carmack Joins Oculus as CTO
milestones.description: id Software's John Carmack — the engineer behind Doom and Quake's real-time 3D engines — resigns to join Oculus VR full-time as CTO after ZeniMax Media, id's parent company, declines to support Oculus. A second engineering lineage (real-time game-engine development) merges into the Sutherland-descended VR hardware track. ZeniMax later sues Oculus and Facebook for trade-secret misappropriation and wins a $500 million judgment.

branch_alternatives.description: ZeniMax, instead of later suing Oculus and Facebook, agrees to formally back and invest in Carmack's Oculus work as an extension of id Software's engine business.
branch_alternatives.requirement: ZeniMax leadership recognizing VR's potential early rather than viewing Carmack's departure as a loss
downstream_effects: No $500 million trade-secret lawsuit and judgment shadow over Oculus's early corporate history
id Software's engine lineage becomes formally, contractually entangled with VR hardware rather than informally connected via one departing employee
Carmack's move from games into VR hardware is remembered as a sanctioned corporate pivot rather than a defection

milestones.label: Facebook Acquires Oculus
milestones.description: Facebook buys Oculus for $2 billion in March 2014. A gaming-hardware Kickstarter startup becomes a subsidiary of a social-media advertising company whose core interest is 'connection,' not gaming — the acquisition that eventually pulls VR into Facebook/Meta's much larger, much stranger metaverse ambitions.

branch_alternatives.description: Oculus goes to a gaming or hardware company instead — Sony, Valve, or Samsung — rather than to Facebook.
branch_alternatives.requirement: A gaming/hardware company outbidding or out-negotiating Facebook, or Facebook's board balking at a $2B price for a company outside its core advertising business
downstream_effects: VR's 2010s corporate patron is a gaming or hardware company, so the product roadmap centers on games and hardware quality rather than 'social presence' and advertising-adjacent engagement metrics
No Meta rebrand follows in 2021, since Facebook never has a VR division to build that bet around
The 'metaverse' as a term and corporate strategy may never coalesce in its historical form, or coalesces around a different company entirely

milestones.label: Consumer VR Launch (Oculus CV1, HTC Vive, PSVR)
milestones.description: Three consumer VR headsets launch within months of each other. Visual VR at consumer price points. Room-scale tracking (Vive) is new; controllers are the interaction paradigm. The Sutherland visual-computational lineage reaches mass-market consumer deployment after 48 years.

milestones.label: Palmer Luckey Ousted from Oculus
milestones.description: Oculus founder Palmer Luckey is forced out of Facebook following revelation of his $10,000 donation to a pro-Trump group that ran a controversial anti-Clinton billboard. Facebook denies the departure was politically motivated. Founder-vs-corporate-parent friction, the same shape this pool's Silicon Valley theme captures later with Kalanick and Neumann.

branch_alternatives.description: Facebook leadership decides the controversy isn't worth losing its most visible technical founder, or Luckey more carefully manages the political fallout, and he stays on.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Facebook leadership prioritizing continuity over reputational caution, or Luckey issuing an earlier, more effective response to the controversy
downstream_effects: Oculus retains more of its founder-driven, gaming-enthusiast culture rather than fully assimilating into Facebook's corporate structure
The founder-ousted-by-corporate-parent pattern has one fewer prominent example in the historical record
Luckey's later defense-technology venture (founded after his historical departure) may not exist in this form, changing the VR-to-defense-tech pipeline this world produces

milestones.label: Facebook Rebrands as Meta
milestones.description: Zuckerberg renames the company Meta, commits its identity to 'the metaverse,' and predicts up to $5 trillion in value by 2030. Horizon Worlds is positioned as the flagship product: a social VR platform where a Quest headset and a cartoon avatar are meant to make virtual spaces feel like real places. The craze's peak, and the moment 'gaming hardware' and 'social media company' fully merge into a single corporate identity.

branch_alternatives.description: Facebook doesn't rebrand and keeps VR as a subsidiary product line rather than a company-defining bet, judging the metaverse thesis too speculative to stake its identity on.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Zuckerberg or the board judging the metaverse thesis too speculative, especially in a climate of post-Cambridge-Analytica reputational caution
downstream_effects: Reality Labs' spending stays proportionate to a product division rather than scaling to tens of billions in annual investment
No singular 'metaverse craze' moment exists for the wider industry to react to or invest alongside
Meta's later AI pivot, if it happens at all, isn't preceded by a highly visible, name-changing VR retreat, so it reads as a first bet rather than a second one

milestones.label: Reality Labs' Losses Mount, AI Pivot Begins
milestones.description: Reality Labs racks up close to $90 billion in cumulative operating losses since 2020. By late 2024, executives have quietly stopped saying 'metaverse' on earnings calls. Layoffs, VR studio closures, and spending cuts of up to 30% follow as resources shift toward AI. The craze visibly abating — not a single event but a multi-year deflation, the mirror image of the Meta rebrand's 2021 peak.

milestones.label: Apple Vision Pro
milestones.description: Apple launches the Vision Pro at $3,499 — ultra-high-fidelity visual display, spatial computing, eye and hand tracking, passthrough AR/MR. Repositioned as 'spatial computer,' not headset. The culmination of the Sutherland lineage as pure optical hardware. No somatic channels; purely optical presence. Arrives in the same year Meta's Reality Labs losses are mounting and a full two years before generative world models and a second Meta reversal on Horizon Worlds extend this pool's timeline further still.

milestones.label: Genie and the Generative World Model (DeepMind)
milestones.description: Google DeepMind releases Genie (2024), the first 'generative interactive environment,' trained unsupervised on unlabeled internet video, producing action-controllable virtual worlds from a text prompt, photo, or sketch. Genie 2 (December 2024) extends this to photorealistic, persistent 3D environments with consistent object behavior; Genie 3 (2025) generates real-time, explorable worlds at 720p/24fps with multi-minute consistency from a simple text description. For the first time in this pool's history, the environment itself — not the display, not the interface — is a generated, stochastic, per-session artifact rather than a hand-built 3D asset or a captured filmed space. The frame-by-frame generation process, and DeepMind's own description of it as producing 'worlds,' echoes BEFLIX's 1963 fusion of cinematic and computational vocabulary, sixty years later and at a wholly different order of scale.

branch_alternatives.description: A hardware maker integrates a Genie-class generative world model directly into a consumer VR headset as its primary content-creation engine, replacing hand-authored 3D scenes with prompted, on-demand generated environments.
branch_alternatives.requirement: A headset maker partners with or licenses a Genie-class model and solves the real-time-generation-plus-headset-latency problem
downstream_effects: VR content creation shifts from 3D modeling and game-engine pipelines toward prompting, changing who can author VR experiences and what skills that requires
The distinction between 'watching' and 'building' a virtual world collapses, since the world regenerates live in response to the user's presence and actions
VR's decades-long promise of endlessly variable, responsive worlds is finally met by generative software rather than better hardware

milestones.label: World Labs and Spatial Intelligence (Fei-Fei Li)
milestones.description: Fei-Fei Li — Stanford computer vision professor, architect of ImageNet, and co-director of Stanford's Human-Centered AI institute — raises $230 million in September 2024 to found World Labs, betting that 'spatial intelligence' is AI's next frontier after language. In November 2025 the company launches Marble, a commercial platform generating exportable 3D environments from text, image, or video prompts. A $1 billion follow-on round, with Autodesk investing $200 million and taking an advisory seat, signals that the incumbent 3D-content-creation industry sees world-generation as displacement, not supplement. Another Stanford-incubated venture, in the same institutional lineage as Terman's students decades earlier, but selling spatial generation rather than hardware.

branch_alternatives.description: Autodesk's advisory stake becomes a full integration, and Marble-style generation is folded directly into mainstream professional 3D content tools (Maya, 3ds Max) rather than remaining a separate consumer/prosumer platform.
branch_alternatives.requirement: Autodesk deciding to cannibalize its own traditional modeling workflow rather than positioning generative world models as a separate product line
downstream_effects: Professional 3D artists' workflow shifts toward prompting and editing generated worlds rather than modeling from scratch, within a few years rather than a decade
World Labs' technology becomes infrastructure inside incumbent software rather than a competing consumer platform, changing who captures the value of the underlying research
Li's 'spatial intelligence' framing gets embedded into mainstream production pipelines rather than staying a research frontier

milestones.label: Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal
milestones.description: In March 2026, Meta announces it is shutting down the VR version of Horizon Worlds as it shifts focus to AI — then reverses the decision within 48 hours after user backlash. The most recent dated event in this pool: the metaverse craze's whiplash coda, five years after the Meta rebrand and squarely in the middle of Reality Labs' sustained retreat. The reversal holds by a thread — user backlash, not a change of strategic heart, is what kept Horizon Worlds alive on VR, and nothing in Meta's public reasoning ruled out revisiting the shutdown later. Whether this reads as the end of 'the metaverse' or merely a contested, temporary pause is left for the story to decide, since this is the last dated event in the pool and nothing follows it to settle the question.
